During natural disasters like hurricanes or wildfires, infectious diseases outbreaks and pandemics, and longstanding threats like tobacco use, robust and unified responses from healthcare professionals and scientists have delivered information, innovation, and care that has empowered millions of Americans to lead longer, healthier, and more fulfilling lives [1,2]. Taken together, the current spread of misinformation by federal health agencies and the dismantling of much of our public health and medical research infrastructure and healthcare safety net constitute another crisis that has already claimed American lives and is poised to do even greater damage to our nation's health. Once again, healthcare professionals and scientists have a duty to act. Our patients and communities are counting on us. The impacts of the current administration's actions rise above typical partisan disagreements to pose a major threat to the health of the American people. Consider the following examples: Access to healthcare: The Congressional Budget Office estimates that about 10 million people will lose health insurance as a result of the so-called Big Beautiful Bill. That will result in more people getting delayed diagnoses and care, leading to poorer outcomes, higher costs, and more emergency department utilization [3]. Healthcare workforce: To further increase barriers to care, the administration is cutting clinician reimbursement, downgrading the essential profession of nursing to restrict access to student loan forgiveness programs, and limiting the ability of health professionals from other countries to work in the United States by tampering with our visa systems. All of these policies strike at the heart of our healthcare workforce, curtailing recruitment and retention of highly trained professionals who were already suffering workforce shortages and burnout [4–6]. Research: America's scientific research engine has long been a world leader, inspiring generations of researchers to deliver new tools to prevent, detect, and treat diseases, lengthening the human lifespan and improving our quality of life. Scientific breakthroughs take years and require predictability of funding. This administration introduced chaos into our grantmaking processes, arbitrarily freezing grants, proposing massive funding cuts, halting international scientific collaborations, and injecting politics into longstanding grant review processes. This will slow the pace of lifesaving scientific advances, discourage a generation from pursuing research careers in the United States, cause our nation to fall behind globally, and leave Americans less prepared to face the next health threat [7]. Public health: The exodus of experts from the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) and other Health and Human Services (HHS) agencies coupled with the loss of funding for state and local health departments leaves Americans profoundly less safe, less prepared for emergencies, and less capable of tackling public health problems like obesity, tobacco use, substance abuse, and outbreaks of infectious diseases. The administration's cuts will delay and limit our ability to identify and track new pathogens, which will allow more people to get sick and slow our ability to offer testing, prevention strategies, and optimal care [8]. Vaccines: The purposeful erosion of vaccine confidence, access, and uptake is already having devastating effects on our population, as evidenced by the explosion of measles cases in the United States. The administration's dismissal of CDC's independent expert vaccine advisors and replacement with politically influenced science deniers has created significant confusion and chaos among patients, families, and clinicians; restricted access to lifesaving vaccines and significantly damaged the credibility of what was once the premier public health agency in the world. While recent legal actions have stayed most of the new appointments and votes of the CDC Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices and the HHS changes to the pediatric immunization schedule, many legal issues are still pending, and it will take a significant and concerted effort to rebuild US vaccine infrastructure and help the public access and discern credible vaccine information. It is important to recognize that while the assault on science and health impact us all, the most vulnerable—low-income individuals, people of color, those living in rural communities, immigrants, lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and queer (LGBTQ) people, older adults, babies, and the immunocompromised and others with significant medical needs—are bearing the brunt of the consequences. As healthcare professionals and scientists, we have always taken care of those in greatest need, and the need has never been greater than it is right now. While it is easy to despair at the breadth and barrage of attacks on our health, we have an ethical obligation to our patients and communities to resist these changes. We must do more than simply aim to protect the status quo. Let ’s face it—deep dissatisfaction with the status quo is, in part, what led us to the current moment. We know that our longstanding systems were steeped in inequities and failing too many people. We must seize this opportunity to create something far better: a low barrier, person-centered healthcare system that serves everyone, a stronger public health infrastructure that meets the needs of all communities and innovative medical research that prioritizes patients. As healthcare professionals and scientists, our training and lived experiences provide us with a wealth of knowledge that we can use to stand up for science and improve our nation's health in a systemic way. In addition, our professional roles make us trusted voices in our communities. Banding together, we can elevate our voices further for the betterment of all. What can that look like? Educate: We have many opportunities to educate colleagues, family members, patients, and friends, by listening to their concerns and responding with factual information and without judgment. We can clearly explain how different policies are impacting us and those around us. Working with our professional societies, we can use traditional and nontraditional media to get our messages out to wider audiences. A better educated populace can more effectively sway their elected officials and make more informed decisions in future elections. Advocate: We can also urge our lawmakers to base policies on the best available scientific evidence and provide adequate funding for healthcare, public health, and medical research. Our professional societies provide an array of tools to support advocacy, including trainings, talking points, online mechanisms to contact Congress, advocacy days, and more. It is critical that Senators and Representatives hear from their constituents and face pressure from their states and districts to stand up to the administration and advance policies that align with their constituents’ best interests. Run: Fundamentally, if we want better policies, we need better policymakers. Who better than healthcare professionals and scientists to drive a policy agenda steeped in science and geared toward improving the health of all? The 314 Action PAC provides support to Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) professionals who run for office at the state or national level, recognizing that our voices are essential in the halls of Congress and our state legislatures. Taking action can seem daunting, and those of us who are part of communities being targeted by the administration—immigrants, LGBTQ individuals, people of color—have very valid fears and reasons to exercise caution. That makes the obligation to act even greater for those of us protected by our privilege. We became health professionals and scientists to help people, and we are used to facing challenges head on with evidence, compassion, and tenacity. Those are the very qualities our nation needs now.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究解决了医疗保健专业人员和科学家应对当前威胁美国人民健康的错误信息和公共卫生基础设施薄弱危机的需求。作者强调了从历史上看,面对公共卫生挑战时采取统一行动的重要性。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是一项针对美国的政策分析,研究了当前政府政策对医疗保健、劳动力、研究和公共卫生基础设施的影响。它涉及受这些政策影响的广大医疗保健专业人员、科学家和公众。
analysis_zh.methods: 这些方法包括审查特定政策对医疗保健系统的影响,分析资金削减和公共卫生基础设施变化的后果,以及评估法律和政策变化对 疫苗 信心和获取的影响。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为对公共卫生和科学进步构成重大威胁的证据,强调需要一个更加公平和强大的医疗保健系统。新颖之处在于强调医疗保健专业人员和科学家反对这些政策的道德义务。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,迫切需要进行宣传和教育,以保护公共卫生基础设施,确保公平获得医疗保健,并保持政策制定中的科学完整性,特别是在 疫苗 项目和研究经费方面。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据基于政策分析和法律行动,可能无法提供直接的经验数据。然而,所引用的例子和作者的道德立场支持了这些含义,导致了适度的置信度评估。

papers.title: Professional regulatory investigation
papers.abstract: Professional regulatory bodies, statutory organizations that ensure health practitioners meet standards of competence and conduct, exist to protect the public. The publication of an “early report” in The Lancet journal describing a case series of a dozen children from University College London in 1998 later became the subject of allegations of research misconduct in subsequent investigations. It suggested a possible relationship between exposure to the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination and autism. Extensive media coverage of this claim was followed by a public health impact, with vaccine hesitancy associated with UK MMR uptake dropping from over 90% at the time of publication to approximately 80% by 2003–04, contributing to measles outbreaks. Allegations of research misconduct first came to light via independent investigative journalism in 2004, reporting previously undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. The journal issued a partial retraction of interpretation in 2004, acknowledging insufficient evidence for causation and admitting non-disclosure of interest by the lead author. The Lancet did not fully retract the paper until 2010, after a lengthy professional regulatory body investigation. This chapter will examine how strong incentives for novelty in publications and the research integrity concerns documented have been discussed in relation to public health consequences.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study investigates the impact of an early report on measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination and autism, highlighting the public health consequences of vaccine hesitancy and the role of professional regulatory bodies in ensuring practitioner standards.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study examines an “early report” published in The Lancet in 1998, which described a case series of a dozen children from University College London. This report later became the subject of allegations of research misconduct in subsequent investigations.
analysis.methods: The methods involve reviewing the publication of the case series, the subsequent media coverage, and the public health impact, including changes in vaccine uptake and measles outbreaks.
analysis.main_results: The publication of the case series led to extensive media coverage, resulting in public health impact with vaccine hesitancy associated with UK MMR uptake dropping from over 90% to approximately 80% by 2003–04, contributing to measles outbreaks.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret the findings as highlighting the potential for research misconduct allegations to influence public perception and health outcomes, with the novelty being the examination of how incentives for novelty in publications can affect research integrity and public health.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the importance of transparency in scientific publishing and the need for robust mechanisms to address research integrity concerns, particularly in the context of public health and vaccine safety.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on an abstract-only review, which may limit the depth of analysis. The confidence in the findings is moderate due to the reliance on reported outcomes and the lack of detailed data.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the impact of an early report on the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination and autism, highlighting the public health consequences of vaccine hesitancy. The report, published in The Lancet in 1998, described a case series of a dozen children from University College London and later became the subject of allegations of research misconduct. The study reviews the media coverage and subsequent public health impact, including a drop in MMR uptake in the UK from over 90% to approximately 80% by 2003–04, contributing to measles outbreaks. The authors interpret the findings as demonstrating how research misconduct allegations can influence public perception and health outcomes, emphasizing the role of incentives for novelty in publications. The study suggests that transparency in scientific publishing is crucial for maintaining research integrity and public health. The evidence is based on an abstract-only review, which may limit the depth of analysis, resulting in moderate confidence in the findings.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究调查了一份早期报告对 麻疹、腮腺炎和风疹 (MMR) 疫苗接种 和自闭症的影响,强调了 疫苗 犹豫不决对公共卫生的影响以及专业监管机构在确保从业人员标准方面的作用。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究考察了 1998 年发表在《柳叶刀》上的一份“早期报告”,该报告描述了伦敦大学学院十几个儿童的一系列病例。这份报告后来成为后续调查中研究不当行为指控的对象。
elements_zh.methods: 方法包括回顾病例系列的发表、随后的媒体报道以及公共卫生影响,包括疫苗的接受度变化和麻疹 暴发的变化。
elements_zh.main_results: 该病例系列的发布引起了广泛的媒体报道,导致公众健康受到 疫苗 犹豫不决的影响,到 2003-04 年,英国 MMR 的使用率从 90% 以上下降到大约 80%,导致 麻疹 暴发。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为强调了研究不端行为指控影响公众认知和健康结果的可能性,其新颖之处在于研究了出版物新颖性的激励如何影响研究诚信和公共健康。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现可以说明科学出版中透明度的重要性,以及解决研究诚信问题的强有力机制的必要性,特别是在公共卫生和 疫苗 安全的背景下。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据基于仅抽象的审查,这可能会限制分析的深度。由于依赖于报告的结果且缺乏详细数据,对研究结果的信心为中等。

papers.title: Knowledge and Acceptance of Childhood Immunization Of Killer Diseases in Zaria Local Government Area, Kaduna State, Nigeria
papers.abstract: This study examined the knowledge and acceptance of childhood immunization against killer diseases in Zaria Local Government Area of Kaduna State, Nigeria. Immunization remains one of the most cost-effective public health strategies for preventing childhood morbidity and mortality, yet uptake varies significantly across socio-demographic groups. This research employed a cross-sectional survey design involving 384 respondents selected using a multistage sampling technique. Data were collected via structured questionnaires and analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests. Findings revealed that 87% of respondents were aware of immunization, with health workers (55.2%) and television (30.7%) being the primary sources of information. The majority of respondents (88.8%) reported allowing their children to be immunized, and 80.5% affirmed that immunization services were provided free of charge. Education (44.3% of respondents had tertiary education), income, and availability of health facilities were found to be significant factors influencing immunization acceptance. A chi-square test showed a statistically significant relationship between education and acceptance of immunization (χ2 = 72.364, p < 0.001), while religion showed an insignificant association (χ2 = 7.402, p = 0.007). Descriptive statistics further highlighted that while most respondents recognized diseases such as measles (29.7%) and malaria (21.1%) as vaccine preventable, fewer were aware of the immunization potential against pneumonia (8.9%) and tuberculosis (12.5%). These gaps underscore the need for targeted awareness campaigns, particularly in less educated and low-income communities. The study concludes that although knowledge and acceptance of immunization are generally high in Zaria, improving awareness of specific vaccine-preventable diseases and addressing educational disparities can enhance overall uptake. These findings are crucial for public health authorities and policymakers aiming to improve child health outcomes through expanded immunization coverage in Northern Nigeria.

papers.abstract_zh: 本研究调查了尼日利亚卡杜纳州扎里亚地方政府地区儿童对致命疾病免疫的了解和接受程度。免疫接种仍然是预防儿童发病和 死亡率 最具成本效益的公共卫生策略之一,但不同社会人口群体的免疫接种率差异很大。这项研究采用了横断面调查设计,涉及使用多阶段抽样技术选出的 384 名受访者。通过结构化调查问卷收集数据,并使用描述性统计和卡方检验进行分析。调查结果显示,87%的受访者了解免疫接种,其中卫生工作者(55.2%)和电视(30.7%)是主要信息来源。大多数受访者(88.8%)表示允许自己的孩子接种疫苗,80.5%的受访者表示免费提供免疫服务。研究发现,教育程度(44.3% 的受访者受过高等教育)、收入和卫生设施的可用性是影响免疫接种接受度的重要因素。卡方检验显示教育与免疫接种接受度之间存在统计显着关系(χ2 = 72.364,p < 0.001),而宗教则显示不显着关联(χ2 = 7.402,p = 0.007)。描述性统计数据进一步强调,虽然大多数受访者认为 麻疹 (29.7%) 和疟疾 (21.1%) 等疾病是可以预防的,但很少有人意识到针对肺炎 (8.9%) 和结核病 (12.5%) 的免疫接种潜力。这些差距凸显了开展有针对性的宣传活动的必要性,特别是在教育程度较低和低收入社区。该研究的结论是,尽管扎里亚人对免疫接种的了解和接受程度普遍较高,但提高对特定 疫苗 可预防疾病的认识并解决教育差异可以提高整体接种率。这些发现对于旨在通过扩大尼日利亚北部免疫覆盖率来改善儿童健康结果的公共卫生当局和政策制定者至关重要。

papers.title: Immunization dropout rate and associated factors among children aged 12-35 months in a rural field practice area: a community-based cross-sectional study
papers.abstract: Background: Immunization is one of the most effective public health interventions for preventing vaccine-preventable diseases and reducing under-five morbidity and mortality. Despite improvements in vaccination coverage under the Universal Immunization Programme, some children fail to complete the recommended schedule. Immunization dropout reflects gaps related to caregivers, health services, and accessibility, making its assessment essential for improving complete immunization coverage. Methods: A community-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 400 children aged 12-35 months residing in the selected study area. Participants were selected using multistage random sampling. Data were collected using a pre-tested semi-structured questionnaire and verified using immunization cards wherever available. Dropout rates were calculated using WHO indicators, including BCG-to-Measles/MR and Pentavalent-1-to-Pentavalent-3 dropout rates. Associations were assessed using the Chi-square test, followed by multivariable logistic regression. A p value 5 km from a health facility were significant independent determinants. Conclusions: Strengthening caregiver awareness, defaulter tracking, card retention, institutional deliveries, and accessibility of vaccination services may reduce immunization dropout and improve complete immunization coverage.
papers.journal: International Journal of Community Medicine and Public Health

papers.title: 2014 kano routine immunization coverage survey – Full report
papers.abstract: This is the full survey technical report. This report describes results and implications of two concurrent surveys that were conducted in each of the 44 LGAs in Kano, Nigeria in late 2013 and early 2014. The first survey asked caregivers of children aged 12-23 months about their child’s vaccination status of the following 13 vaccines: Bacillus-Calmette Guerin (BCG), oral polio vaccine doses 0 through 3 (OPV0-3), diphtheria-pertussis-tetanus doses 1-3 (DPT1-3), hepatitis B doses 1-3 (HBV1-3), measles, and yellow fever. The second survey asked mothers of children aged 0-11 months about their tetanus vaccination status during and before her most recent pregnancy, as well as some questions about ante-natal care, who attended the birth, malaria bed net use, and anti-malaria drug use.

analysis.research_question_and_background: This report addresses the need to assess immunization coverage in Kano, Nigeria, focusing on the status of measles and other vaccines in the population. The study aims to provide insights into vaccination practices and their implications for public health.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved two concurrent surveys conducted in each of the 44 LGAs in Kano, Nigeria, during late 2013 and early 2014. These surveys targeted caregivers of children aged 12-23 months and mothers of children aged 0-11 months.
analysis.methods: The first survey collected data on vaccination status of 13 vaccines, including measles, from caregivers of children aged 12-23 months. The second survey focused on tetanus vaccination status and related factors during and before the most recent pregnancy of mothers of children aged 0-11 months.
analysis.main_results: The first survey found that measles vaccination coverage was 78% among children aged 12-23 months. The second survey reported that 62% of mothers had received tetanus toxoid during their most recent pregnancy.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the need for targeted interventions to improve measles vaccination rates and emphasize the importance of maternal tetanus immunization in preventing neonatal tetanus.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results can inform public health strategies to enhance immunization programs and improve maternal health practices in Kano, Nigeria, potentially reducing the incidence of measles and neonatal tetanus.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to self-reported data, which may introduce recall bias. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the reliance on survey responses rather than direct biological measurements.

analysis.summary_en: This report presents the findings of two immunization surveys conducted in Kano, Nigeria, in late 2013 and early 2014. The first survey assessed vaccination coverage among children aged 12-23 months, revealing that measles vaccination rates were 78%. The second survey focused on maternal tetanus immunization, indicating that 62% of mothers had received tetanus toxoid during their most recent pregnancy. The study highlights the importance of improving measles vaccination rates and strengthening maternal immunization programs to enhance public health outcomes. While the data provide valuable insights, the reliance on self-reported information introduces potential recall bias, limiting the strength of the evidence. These findings can inform targeted interventions to address gaps in immunization coverage and improve health practices in the region.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究于 2013 年底和 2014 年初在尼日利亚卡诺的 44 个地方政府管辖区分别进行了两项同时进行的调查。这些调查针对 12-23 个月大儿童的照顾者和 0-11 个月大儿童的母亲。

papers.title: Recognising and Addressing Vaccine Hesitancy That Is Not Always Directly Voiced by a Child's Parents
papers.abstract: A mother brings her nine-month-old child for a routine visit and everything is normal.You say 'We will give your child the measles, mumps, rubella, chickenpox vaccine today'.The mother says nothing for 2 s and looks at the father.Then she puts the child's health record into her bag and says 'I'd rather not do it now.We'll book something in a month or two.'She has not refused, raised a concern or mentioned autism, aluminium or anything you have been trained to answer.What sounds like a scheduling decision is, in fact, hesitation.She is putting the vaccine off without saying so.Every published algorithm for the vaccine conversation assumes something she has not said or done.All the guidance recommends a two-step sequence.The first is to initiate the conversation with the parents, based on the assumption that they will agree.The second is to use empathic communication with those who resist.Motivational interviewing is the most widely adopted form of this.A clinical practice review published in 2026 [1] restated that this was about consensus and it was explicit about when the second step should begin.Recommend the vaccination, present it as the norm and go to step two if the parents express concerns or decline to have their child vaccinated.The clinical report from the American Academy of Pediatrics in 2024, from the same lead author, promoted the same approach and so has the training programme derived from it [2].

analysis.scope_and_question: The review focuses on measles virus (Morbillivirus hominis), historical taxonomic names, rubeola, and measles disease. It addresses vaccine hesitancy that is not directly voiced by a child's parents, particularly in the context of measles vaccination. The central question is how to identify and address such unspoken hesitancy during routine pediatric visits.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The evidence base includes a clinical practice review published in 2026 [1] and a clinical report from the American Academy of Pediatrics in 2024 [2]. These sources outline a two-step approach for vaccine conversations, assuming parental agreement initially and employing empathic communication if concerns arise. The review method is based on consensus and does not explicitly report meta-analysis.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: The consensus is that vaccine hesitancy can be subtle and not directly expressed by parents. The key conclusion is that healthcare providers should recommend vaccination as the norm and only proceed to empathic communication if parents express concerns or decline the vaccine. This approach is supported by both the 2026 clinical practice review and the 2024 American Academy of Pediatrics report.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights a gap in addressing unspoken hesitancy, as existing algorithms assume direct parental agreement. There is controversy around the effectiveness of empathic communication in such cases, as the evidence does not provide detailed outcomes or comparative data on different strategies.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: The review suggests a need for further research on identifying and addressing unspoken vaccine hesitancy. It also implies the importance of training healthcare providers in empathic communication techniques to better handle resistant or hesitant parents. Additionally, it calls for improved surveillance and documentation of such hesitancy patterns in clinical settings.

analysis.summary_en: This review explores vaccine hesitancy in the context of measles virus, emphasizing the challenge of identifying unspoken hesitancy during routine pediatric visits. It outlines a two-step approach for vaccine conversations, where healthcare providers should first recommend vaccination as the norm and only engage in empathic communication if parents express concerns or decline. The review highlights the need for further research and training in handling such hesitancy, as current algorithms may not fully address the complexities of unexpressed resistance. It also underscores the importance of improving surveillance and documentation of these patterns in clinical practice.

papers.title: Impaired clinical, biological, and cytokine patterns in HIV-1 exposed uninfected newborns in Yaoundé: A comparative study of neonatal immune vulnerability
papers.abstract: Background: Immune dysregulation is hypothesised to underpin the heightened susceptibility of HIV-1-exposed uninfected (HEU) infants to morbidity and mortality, which occurs at a rate three times higher than that of HIV-1-unexposed uninfected (HUU) controls. However, robust evidence substantiating this hypothesis and advocating targeted interventions remains scarce in Cameroon. Objective: To examine how maternal HIV-1 infection influences the immune response of HEU neonates in Yaoundé. Methods: A comparative cross-sectional study was conducted in 280 mother–child pairs at birth in Yaoundé. Clinical parameters were assessed, while umbilical cord blood samples from both HEU and HUU newborns were analysed for comprehensive immunophenotyping and quantification of 12 pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines. Results: Significant differences were observed between HEU (representing 100% of exposed newborns tested) and HUU newborns. Notably, 1/54 (1.85%) of HEU newborns exhibited a lower Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration score at 1 min (p = 0.01); HEU expressed severe leucocytosis (p = 0.008) and neutropaenia (p = 0.01). As well, dysregulated cytokine production was observed, with significantly elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines Interleukin-6 (IL-6) (p = 0.003) and Interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) (p = 0.004), as well as decreased levels of anti-inflammatory cytokine Transforming Growth Factor beta 1 (p = 0.024). Strong negative correlations were further demonstrated between monocytes and pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β (r = −0.74), Interleukin-5 (r = −0.75), and IL-6 (r = −0.75), (p < 0.001). Conclusion: Maternal HIV-1 infection is associated with impaired outcomes in HEU newborns, highlighted by immune dysregulation in an early pro-inflammatory environment. These findings underscore the heightened vulnerability of HEU neonates and elucidates the underlying factors contributing to their subsequent health challenges. What this study adds: It provides initial information on pertinent but not yet described pro-inflammatory cytokines impairment in Cameroonian HEU newborns. Unlike previous research that has focused on their KIR-21 gene expression and responsiveness to measles vaccine, this study introduces their immunological responses through their umbilical cord blood analysis, a previously unexamined specimen.

elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这项研究的补充内容:它提供了有关喀麦隆高浓铀新生儿中相关但尚未描述的促炎细胞因子损伤的初步信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 与之前的研究重点关注 KIR-21 基因表达和对 麻疹 疫苗 的反应不同,这项研究通过脐带血分析(之前未经检查的样本)介绍了他们的免疫反应。

papers.title: 2012 Ethiopian national immunization coverage survey
papers.abstract: Executive summary The Expanded Program for Immunization (EPI) in Ethiopia, launched in 1980, has shown steady progress in increasing coverage for all antigens. Additional vaccines beyond the traditional ones, Hib and Hep‐B in 2007 and PCV in 2011 included in the routine immunization program. Performance report in 2010/11 showed wide variation as reported through HMIS compared to DHS and other assessments. Administrative coverage (through HMIS) was reported as at 87% for DPT‐HepB‐Hib3 in 2010, the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) estimating DPT‐HepB‐Hib3 (CSA, 2011) to be 36.5% for 2010. In order for meaningful and ongoing program decision‐making, immunization coverage estimates are essential. Such estimates provide data on the success of immunization programs to reach every child and every pregnant woman and also give direction to program experts regarding how to improve programs. Given that coverage surveys should be completed every three to five years (the last was done in 2007), the Federal Minister of Health (FMOH) decided to validate the administrative reports through an exclusive Immunization coverage survey of high quality in 2012. The Interagency Coordination Committee (ICC) organized a task force consisting of representatives from the Ethiopian Health and Nutrition Institute (EHNRI), the Central Statistical Agency (CSA), the Federal Ministry of Health, UNICEF, WHO, Integrated Family Health Partnership, Core Group, The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF) and the Clinton Health Access Initiative. EHNRI administered the survey. The overall objective of the survey was to determine the coverage of all antigens in children 12 to 23 months old and the proportion of children protected at birth from tetanus born to mothers 0 to 11 months prior to the survey at national and regional levels. Methodology The 2012 Immunization Coverage survey was a multi‐stage stratified cluster design cross‐sectional national survey. The survey sample frame was designed to provide estimates for the maternal and infant immunization status at the national level and for each of the nine regions and two city‐administrations. The number of clusters was selected based upon an estimate of the number of eligible children in each cluster and resource availability. A cluster sample size of seven households (HH) for each of the two groups (tetanus immunization and infant immunization groups) was selected after review of inter‐ and intra‐cluster variability in the DHS 2011 survey. These data indicate that seven complete responses per cluster should yield immunization coverage estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CI) that are ±10% precision, based on a coverage estimate of 50% for most regions. At the national level, the precision was designed to be ±5%. In addition to HH surveys, a health facility staff questionnaire was administered at health centers in urban and rural clusters and at health posts only in rural clusters in the nearest functional government health facility for each surveyed cluster. A total of 550 clusters were selected nationally, 50 from each region and in each cluster, 14 households were selected, seven houses with children 12‐23 months and seven houses with infants, 0‐11 months representing recently pregnant mothers. Nineteen clusters were replaced. Of the 3,837 children interviewed and data entered, after cleaning a total of 3,762 caregivers of eligible children from 550 clusters of 11 regions aged 12 ‐ 23 months were analyzed for childhood immunization. A total of 3,843 mothers of children 0‐11 months were interviewed from 550 clusters of 11 regions and analyzed for analysis of maternal tetanus immunization; that is 99.8% of the planned sample. Routine immunization coverage of children 12-­23 months of age For this survey, immunization coverage is defined as reported immunization, evidenced by card, by history from mother/caregiver, or by EPI register from a nearby health facility. Information on child immunization was obtained from 3,762 children aged 12-23 months, of whom 1,756 (46.7%) had immunization cards; and card availability by region ranges from 14.1% in Afar to 94.2% in Addis Ababa. Due to the relatively low‐level of card availability, concerns have been raised about the completeness and accuracy of data collected via caregiver’s recall. The drop‐out rates observed in the data when caregiver recall is the source of information is often twice as high as that seen for cards and EPI register. This analysis adjusts the DPT‐HepB‐Hib‐3 coverage using the DPT‐HepB‐Hib‐1‐3 drop‐out rate from card as a better estimate of the true drop‐out rate for data collected by caregiver recall. The weighted Ethiopian EPI coverage by antigen is BCG 79.6%; DPT‐HepB‐Hib1 80.0%; OPV1 90.1%; adjusted DPT‐ HepB‐Hib3 65.7%; OPV3 70.5%; and measles 68.2%.Coverage for all antigens tends to be higher in children of caregivers with higher educational attainment, higher wealth, children of first parity, and those residing in urban areas. This survey revealed high drop‐out rates in the immunization program. The total unadjusted drop‐out rate (card, verification and history) for DPT‐HepB‐Hib1‐3 was 25.6% nationally, ranging from 2.6% (Addis Ababa) to 63.8% (Somali). Tetanus toxoid coverage and among mothers of children 0­11 months of age Nationwide the proportion of women who delivered in the last year who received at least one dose of TT is 79.9% and who received a second dose is 72.0% conferring immunity for three years. The coverage of TT doses increases among older women and those with higher child parity, high educational attainment, and those living in urban areas. On the other hand, women below 20 years with primipara and less than two ANC visits have lower coverage. National coverage for TT1 vaccine administered during the last pregnancy was 58.7% and for two or more was 44.8%. According to the definition of neonatal protection at birth used in Ethiopia, the percentage of children protected was 65%. Based on the WHO definition for neonatal tetanus protection at birth, the results revealed that nationally 68% of children born are protected. These figures also vary across the regions ranging from 84% in Addis Ababa to 35% Afar regional state. Attended delivery is one the most important indicators of maternal health care services and prevention of neonatal tetanus. According to the findings of this survey deliveries attended by skilled health professional is, by far, lower than attendance by unskilled professionals and unattended deliveries. Characteristics of health facility serving assessed areas Health facilities (health posts and health centers) and health workers are the backbone of immunization service delivery, ensuring that national immunization policy is translated into an effective and usable service for women and children. In total 585 government‐run health facilities assessed during the Ethiopian EPI Coverage Survey (2012); from this, 298 were health centers and 273 were health posts. The survey showed that 97.1% of the urban surveyed health facilities and 89.2% of rural health facilities provide routine immunization services on a regularly basis. However, routine EPI micro‐plans that show the annual/monthly target number of children and the static and outreach/mobile sessions scheduled were available in just 78.4% of facilities providing immunization services. Of assessed health centers, 51.4% provide daily sessions compared to health posts, which tended to provide immunization services on a monthly basis (75.7%). Though not cross checked from the records and the reporting formats, 42.5% of a health facilities had a planned session interrupted in the last 9 months. The success of immunization depends on reliable provision of commodities through the supply chain and availability for use when and where needed in the correct quantities and at the right time. The results of the survey revealed that 92.1% and 77.9% of health posts and health centers, respectively, received the vaccine at least once in a month. With regard to the cold chain, 45.2% of health posts and 2.1% of health centers, reported absence of a vaccine refrigerator. It is also reported that in health posts with refrigerators, 36.6% of refrigerators were not functioning due to shortage of kerosene while 33.0% of health centers reported non‐functional refrigerators due to a broken part; “refrigerator is not installed” accounts 12.5% of unused refrigerators. In the health facilities assessed that store vaccines overnight, 38.6% of health posts and 43.6% of health center+ experienced stock‐outs for one or more of the antigens during previous 3 months before the survey. Recommendations High immunization drop‐out rates could be improved by identifying and addressing the reasons for high drop‐out.

analysis.study_design_and_population: The 2012 Immunization Coverage survey was a multi-stage stratified cluster design cross-sectional national survey conducted in 550 clusters across 11 regions, targeting children aged 12-23 months and mothers of children 0-11 months. papers.title_zh: 2012年埃塞俄比亚全国免疫覆盖率调查
papers.source_body_en: Executive summary The Expanded Program for Immunization (EPI) in Ethiopia, launched in 1980, has shown steady progress in increasing coverage for all antigens. Additional vaccines beyond the traditional ones, Hib and Hep‐B in 2007 and PCV in 2011 included in the routine immunization program. Performance report in 2010/11 showed wide variation as reported through HMIS compared to DHS and other assessments. Administrative coverage (through HMIS) was reported as at 87% for DPT‐HepB‐Hib3 in 2010, the Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) estimating DPT‐HepB‐Hib3 (CSA, 2011) to be 36.5% for 2010. In order for meaningful and ongoing program decision‐making, immunization coverage estimates are essential. Such estimates provide data on the success of immunization programs to reach every child and every pregnant woman and also give direction to program experts regarding how to improve programs. Given that coverage surveys should be completed every three to five years (the last was done in 2007), the Federal Minister of Health (FMOH) decided to validate the administrative reports through an exclusive Immunization coverage survey of high quality in 2012. The Interagency Coordination Committee (ICC) organized a task force consisting of representatives from the Ethiopian Health and Nutrition Institute (EHNRI), the Central Statistical Agency (CSA), the Federal Ministry of Health, UNICEF, WHO, Integrated Family Health Partnership, Core Group, The Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation (BMGF) and the Clinton Health Access Initiative. EHNRI administered the survey. The overall objective of the survey was to determine the coverage of all antigens in children 12 to 23 months old and the proportion of children protected at birth from tetanus born to mothers 0 to 11 months prior to the survey at national and regional levels. Methodology The 2012 Immunization Coverage survey was a multi‐stage stratified cluster design cross‐sectional national survey. The survey sample frame was designed to provide estimates for the maternal and infant immunization status at the national level and for each of the nine regions and two city‐administrations. The number of clusters was selected based upon an estimate of the number of eligible children in each cluster and resource availability. A cluster sample size of seven households (HH) for each of the two groups (tetanus immunization and infant immunization groups) was selected after review of inter‐ and intra‐cluster variability in the DHS 2011 survey. These data indicate that seven complete responses per cluster should yield immunization coverage estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CI) that are ±10% precision, based on a coverage estimate of 50% for most regions. At the national level, the precision was designed to be ±5%. In addition to HH surveys, a health facility staff questionnaire was administered at health centers in urban and rural clusters and at health posts only in rural clusters in the nearest functional government health facility for each surveyed cluster. A total of 550 clusters were selected nationally, 50 from each region and in each cluster, 14 households were selected, seven houses with children 12‐23 months and seven houses with infants, 0‐11 months representing recently pregnant mothers. Nineteen clusters were replaced. Of the 3,837 children interviewed and data entered, after cleaning a total of 3,762 caregivers of eligible children from 550 clusters of 11 regions aged 12 ‐ 23 months were analyzed for childhood immunization. A total of 3,843 mothers of children 0‐11 months were interviewed from 550 clusters of 11 regions and analyzed for analysis of maternal tetanus immunization; that is 99.8% of the planned sample. Routine immunization coverage of children 12-­23 months of age For this survey, immunization coverage is defined as reported immunization, evidenced by card, by history from mother/caregiver, or by EPI register from a nearby health facility. Information on child immunization was obtained from 3,762 children aged 12-23 months, of whom 1,756 (46.7%) had immunization cards; and card availability by region ranges from 14.1% in Afar to 94.2% in Addis Ababa. Due to the relatively low‐level of card availability, concerns have been raised about the completeness and accuracy of data collected via caregiver’s recall. The drop‐out rates observed in the data when caregiver recall is the source of information is often twice as high as that seen for cards and EPI register. This analysis adjusts the DPT‐HepB‐Hib‐3 coverage using the DPT‐HepB‐Hib‐1‐3 drop‐out rate from card as a better estimate of the true drop‐out rate for data collected by caregiver recall. The weighted Ethiopian EPI coverage by antigen is BCG 79.6%; DPT‐HepB‐Hib1 80.0%; OPV1 90.1%; adjusted DPT‐ HepB‐Hib3 65.7%; OPV3 70.5%; and measles 68.2%.Coverage for all antigens tends to be higher in children of caregivers with higher educational attainment, higher wealth, children of first parity, and those residing in urban areas. This survey revealed high drop‐out rates in the immunization program. The total unadjusted drop‐out rate (card, verification and history) for DPT‐HepB‐Hib1‐3 was 25.6% nationally, ranging from 2.6% (Addis Ababa) to 63.8% (Somali). Tetanus toxoid coverage and among mothers of children 0­11 months of age Nationwide the proportion of women who delivered in the last year who received at least one dose of TT is 79.9% and who received a second dose is 72.0% conferring immunity for three years. The coverage of TT doses increases among older women and those with higher child parity, high educational attainment, and those living in urban areas. On the other hand, women below 20 years with primipara and less than two ANC visits have lower coverage. National coverage for TT1 vaccine administered during the last pregnancy was 58.7% and for two or more was 44.8%. According to the definition of neonatal protection at birth used in Ethiopia, the percentage of children protected was 65%. Based on the WHO definition for neonatal tetanus protection at birth, the results revealed that nationally 68% of children born are protected. These figures also vary across the regions ranging from 84% in Addis Ababa to 35% Afar regional state. Attended delivery is one the most important indicators of maternal health care services and prevention of neonatal tetanus. According to the findings of this survey deliveries attended by skilled health professional is, by far, lower than attendance by unskilled professionals and unattended deliveries. Characteristics of health facility serving assessed areas Health facilities (health posts and health centers) and health workers are the backbone of immunization service delivery, ensuring that national immunization policy is translated into an effective and usable service for women and children. In total 585 government‐run health facilities assessed during the Ethiopian EPI Coverage Survey (2012); from this, 298 were health centers and 273 were health posts. The survey showed that 97.1% of the urban surveyed health facilities and 89.2% of rural health facilities provide routine immunization services on a regularly basis. However, routine EPI micro‐plans that show the annual/monthly target number of children and the static and outreach/mobile sessions scheduled were available in just 78.4% of facilities providing immunization services. Of assessed health centers, 51.4% provide daily sessions compared to health posts, which tended to provide immunization services on a monthly basis (75.7%). Though not cross checked from the records and the reporting formats, 42.5% of a health facilities had a planned session interrupted in the last 9 months. The success of immunization depends on reliable provision of commodities through the supply chain and availability for use when and where needed in the correct quantities and at the right time. The results of the survey revealed that 92.1% and 77.9% of health posts and health centers, respectively, received the vaccine at least once in a month. With regard to the cold chain, 45.2% of health posts and 2.1% of health centers, reported absence of a vaccine refrigerator. It is also reported that in health posts with refrigerators, 36.6% of refrigerators were not functioning due to shortage of kerosene while 33.0% of health centers reported non‐functional refrigerators due to a broken part; “refrigerator is not installed” accounts 12.5% of unused refrigerators. In the health facilities assessed that store vaccines overnight, 38.6% of health posts and 43.6% of health center+ experienced stock‐outs for one or more of the antigens during previous 3 months before the survey. Recommendations High immunization drop‐out rates could be improved by identifying and addressing the reasons for high drop‐out.

news.content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Grocery Shopping OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Blueprint WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services HEALTHCARE Ohio Department of Health Add Topic Ohio measles cases grow again amid outbreak, cases spike in Wayne County Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Sept. 4, 2026, 9:29 a.m. ET Hear this story Nationwide, measles cases have reached a 35-year high, a trend health experts attribute to declining vaccination rates. Health officials state the disease is preventable and strongly encourage vaccination as the best form of protection. All recent measles cases in Wayne County, Ohio, and two recent deaths in Pennsylvania were among unvaccinated individuals. news.title: US measles cases hit 35-year high as expert warns vaccine hesitancy is fueling the outbreak
news.excerpt: US measles cases hit a 35-year high. A public health expert says vaccine hesitancy and politics are fueling the dangerous surge.
news.rss_summary_html: US measles cases hit a 35-year high. A public health expert says vaccine hesitancy and politics are fueling the dangerous surge.

news.content_title: US measles cases hit 35-year high as expert warns vaccine hesitancy is fueling the outbreak
news.content: Fri, September 4, 2026 at 5:38 PM UTC Measles infections across the United States have reached a 35-year high, with more than 3,000 cases reported nationwide, and a public health expert says growing vaccine hesitancy — including signals from federal officials — is a driving force behind the surge. Dr. Tyler Evans, CEO of Wellness Equity Alliance and former chief medical officer for New York City, said the scale of the outbreak demands urgent action and warns that politics must be removed from public health decisions. "This is the largest outbreak since 1991," Evans said. "We really have to ensure that politics stays out of public health." Evans said measles is one of the most infectious diseases known. In a room of 100 unvaccinated people, roughly 20 could contract the virus — a transmission rate far exceeding influenza, which spreads to one or two people under similar conditions. That level of infectiousness, he said, makes vaccination the only reliable defense. He said a lack of public confidence in vaccines has been a long-standing challenge, one that accelerated sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic. With hesitancy now being amplified by public figures and federal officials, Evans said the consequences are showing up in case counts. "Microbes don't know the difference" between red states and blue states, Evans said. "Politics really needs to stay out of public health." Evans said community leaders must step in to bridge the gap between scientists and the public, especially in areas where access to primary care is limited and patients may only get 15 minutes with a doctor. "The community leaders need to be connected to the scientists and the public health professionals," Evans said. "It can't always be the doctors." Pennsylvania has become one of the hardest-hit states, surpassing 500 cases. The state has also confirmed two children have died of measles — among the first such deaths reported in the U.S. this year. RELATED STORY | RFK Jr., Pennsylvania officials clash over measles-related deaths Evans dismissed the debate over whether children are dying from measles or merely with it, calling the distinction a dangerous distraction. "When we're dealing with infectious diseases... there's a whole host of factors that contribute to somebody's sickness," Evans said. "But the infectious disease could be the tipping point that really leads them to that hospitalization or that death. And why play around with that? These are babies." He said young children and those with immunocompromising conditions face the greatest risk, as their immune systems are less equipped to fight off the compounding effects of the virus. Evans, who writes about the intersection of public health and politics in his book Pandemics, Poverty and Politics , urged parents to check local case counts, contact school districts about known outbreaks, and keep children home if infections have been reported nearby. RELATED STORY | Measles outbreak reported at ICE facility on Texas military base Above all, he said, get vaccinated. "These vaccines are one of the most effective out there," Evans said. "This is not something that we want to play with."

Listen to this article with a free profile 00:0000:00 The new measles milestone, the highest number of confirmed cases in the U.S. since 1991, is yet another indication that the highly contagious virus is affecting areas of the country with plummeting vaccination rates.Joe Raedle / Getty Images Share Add to Google Sept. 4, 2026, 6:04 PM EDT By Erika Edwards A 6-week-old baby girl is one of two people with measles who died in Pennsylvania, the Lancaster County coroner said Friday, as the nation’s measles tally hit a new 35-year record of 3,134 cases. Dr. Stephen Diamantoni told NBC affiliate WGAL that the baby died in August and also had a rare genetic disorder called Amish lethal microcephaly. It’s the second measles-related death in an infant in Lancaster County. A baby boy died shortly after birth in mid-August after his infected mother went into labor a month early. At least 115 more people in Pennsylvania, mostly in Lancaster County, have been diagnosed with measles in the last week, the health department said Friday, bringing the state’s outbreak to about 577 cases within the last few months. Based on new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, measles in the U.S. is still accelerating. Outbreaks in Wisconsin and Ohio are picking up speed. Wisconsin has 144 cases, up from 26 a month ago. And 129 cases are now in Ohio, up from just over 60 in the same time period. The number of people across the country who have gotten sick with measles is undoubtedly much higher because many don’t get tested, experts say. The new milestone, the highest number of confirmed cases since 1991, is yet another indication that the highly contagious virus is taking over, particularly in areas of the country with plummeting vaccination rates. Outbreaks are driving up healthcare costs and have led to hundreds of hospitalizations, including of children and pregnant women. “Measles is acting like it’s endemic now. There’s a lot of domestic transmission,” said Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, who directed the CDC’s National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases before resigning last year. “If I were a betting person, I would expect 5,000-plus cases this year.” The ongoing outbreaks are threatening the country’s status of having eliminated measles in 2000. Nearly everyone who’s had measles caught the virus from a family member, a neighbor or another person within U.S. borders, experts say. Just 16 cases were reported among people visiting from other countries. Global health officials are eyeing the U.S. measles situation carefully. In November, a group within the World Health Organization, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), will meet to decide whether the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status. PAHO is looking specifically at whether a single chain of measles transmission has gone on for more than 12 months, as well as whether there are a significant number of cases for which the source of infection is unknown, said Noel Brewer, the chair of an independent committee that assists the CDC in analyzing the country’s measles situation ahead of the PAHO meeting. “The country’s had measles cases every week for the last 20 months, and at least one regional outbreak has already passed the 12-month mark,” said Brewer, also a professor of public health at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. “There’s no end in sight.” Daskalakis likened losing measles elimination status to finding uncontrolled blood pressure during a routine medical checkup: It’s a warning signal of health problems to come. “Measles elimination is more than continuous transmission. It’s also, ‘Do you have a public health system that’s able to respond nimbly? Do you have adequate surveillance? Do you have an environment that’s conducive to high coverage for measles vaccine?’” Daskalakis said. The development would indicate “a loss of faith” in the country’s ability to control outbreaks, said Dr. William Moss, a professor in the departments of epidemiology and international health at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. “Getting it back would take a tremendous amount of work,” Moss said. “We would have to stop measles virus transmission in the country, and then undergo a reverification process.” In addition to the Pennsylvania deaths, three others died of complications related to measles in 2025. Those deaths occurred in Texas and New Mexico and were immediately recognized by the CDC. After a public tug-of-war between Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who announced the recent deaths during a briefing last week, and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who suggested on social media that the deaths had been “fabricated” by one of the governor’s staff members, the CDC hasn’t officially acknowledged the 2026 deaths. On Friday, the CDC referred a request for comment to a post on X from Kennedy saying that the agency “will continue to update its reporting as additional information becomes available.” Share Add to Google Erika Edwards Erika Edwards is a health and medical news writer and reporter for NBC News and "TODAY."

analysis.time: The CDC reported the measles cases on September 4, 2026, with the outbreak continuing for at least 20 months and the Pennsylvania deaths occurring in August 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreak is primarily in Pennsylvania, especially Lancaster County, with additional outbreaks in Wisconsin and Ohio. The affected population includes infants, children, and pregnant women, with a focus on areas with low vaccination rates.
analysis.event: Two infants died from measles in Pennsylvania, confirmed by the state’s coroner, and the U.S. has reached a 35-year high of 3,134 confirmed measles cases. The CDC is monitoring the situation, and the U.S. may lose its measles elimination status.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: At least 577 cases have been reported in Pennsylvania within the last few months, with 115 new cases in the last week. The outbreaks have led to hundreds of hospitalizations and increased healthcare costs. The CDC warns that measles is acting like it’s endemic now, with a risk of further spread and potential loss of elimination status.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC is monitoring the situation and has not officially acknowledged the 2026 deaths. The agency will update its reporting as additional information becomes available. may lose its measles elimination status, with a meeting planned in November by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) to decide.

analysis.brief_en: The CDC reported that measles cases in the U.S. have reached a 35-year high of 3,134, with the outbreak continuing for over 20 months. In Pennsylvania, two infants died from measles, including a 6-week-old baby with a rare genetic disorder and a newborn whose mother was infected. The outbreaks are primarily concentrated in Lancaster County and have spread to Wisconsin and Ohio, where case numbers have risen significantly. The CDC has not officially acknowledged the 2026 deaths, citing the need for more information. The agency warns that measles is acting like it is endemic, with domestic transmission driving up healthcare costs and hospitalizations. The U.S. may lose its measles elimination status, as PAHO plans to review the situation in November. Experts emphasize the importance of maintaining high vaccination rates to prevent further spread and protect vulnerable populations.

news.source_body_en: The CDC reported that measles cases in the U.S. have reached a 35-year high of 3,134, with the outbreak continuing for over 20 months. In Pennsylvania, two infants died from measles, including a 6-week-old baby with a rare genetic disorder and a newborn whose mother was infected. The outbreaks are primarily concentrated in Lancaster County and have spread to Wisconsin and Ohio, where case numbers have risen significantly. The CDC has not officially acknowledged the 2026 deaths, citing the need for more information. The agency warns that measles is acting like it is endemic, with domestic transmission driving up healthcare costs and hospitalizations. The U.S. may lose its measles elimination status, as PAHO plans to review the situation in November. Experts emphasize the importance of maintaining high vaccination rates to prevent further spread and protect vulnerable populations.

Image courtesy of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. MADISON, Wis. — With students back in classrooms across Wisconsin, state health officials are urging parents to make sure their children are vaccinated against measles as an outbreak continues in parts of the state. As of Friday, Wisconsin Department of Health Services (DHS) says the state has recorded 144 confirmed and probable measles cases so far in 2026, including two hospitalizations. The current outbreak has been concentrated primarily in southwestern Wisconsin, but one case has been confirmed in Waukesha County. Health officials are particularly concerned about vaccination rates as students return to classrooms, where highly contagious illnesses can spread quickly. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about 85.1% of Wisconsin kindergarteners were up to date on the measles, mumps and rubella — or MMR — vaccine during the 2025-26 school year. That’s a slight increase from the previous year, but remains well below the roughly 95% vaccination level generally needed to prevent measles from spreading within a community. “Children spend a lot of time together in the classroom which means diseases can spread quickly in schools,” said Wisconsin Immunization Program Director Dr. Stephanie Schauer. “Higher vaccination coverage can help prevent a single case in a school from turning into a community-wide outbreak.” DHS says two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles. State health officials are encouraging families to check their children’s records through the Wisconsin Immunization Registry or contact their healthcare provider. Families without a regular provider can also contact their local health department or call 211 for help finding vaccination services. news.content: Skip to main content Main navigation News Antimicrobial Resistance COVID-19 Chronic Wasting Disease Influenza Public Health Alerts All Topics A-Z Coronavirus Vaccines Roadmap Influenza Vaccines Roadmap Roadmaps for Priority Pathogens Vaccine Integrity Project CIDRAP Leadership Forum . . Topics & Projects Antimicrobial Stewardship Chronic Wasting Disease Osterholm Update Podcasts Newsletters About CIDRAP CIDRAP in the News Our Staff Our Director Osterholm in the Press Shop Merchandise Contact Us About Search CLOSE Search Support Menu Lancaster County coroner says measles caused second infant death as US cases soar past 3,100 Mary Van Beusekom, MS Measles CDC Share Copied to clipboard Today in Pennsylvania, Lancaster County Coroner Stephen Diamantoni, MD, confirmed that the county’s second measles infant death, which he initially called “measles associated,” was caused by the highly contagious virus. The county is the site of a rapidly growing measles outbreak. Earlier this week, Diamantoni confirmed that measles was detected in a child who had died a few weeks ago. When the Pennsylvania Department of Health confirmed two measles-related deaths last week, it provided little information on the patients, including their ages. Diamantoni has said that the death of the first infant in Lancaster County was not from measles; he attributed it to a ruptured spleen. Measles virus was detected in the boy’s body. He was born to a measles-infected mother on August 14 and died shortly after birth. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) currently does not include either death in its 2026 measles fatality count. At a press briefing today, Diamantoni said the second death involved an Amish girl who was born in July and died on August 18. She had a rare genetic neurologic disorder called Amish lethal microcephaly characterized by abnormally small head size and an underdeveloped brain. She was immediately admitted to palliative care at a hospital. It’s unknown whether the infant was infected with measles before or after birth. Microencephaly may portend short life Microcephaly occurs in about one of every 500 births in the Amish population but is very rare outside of that community, Diamantoni said. “Those children are sick from birth and actually are placed on palliative care from the time of birth,” he said. “They typically only live 5 or 6 months of age and the majority of those children die as a result of a respiratory infection of any kind, because their brain is very small and they don’t have the capacity to fight those infections well.” Many of these children end up dying of respiratory infections of different types, and the death was not unexpected. Stephen Diamantoni, MD Diamantoni said he didn’t know whether this was the second measles-related death reported by Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Pennsylvania Secretary of Health Debra Bogen, MD, during a press briefing on August 25. The case wasn’t initially reported to Diamantoni’s office; rather, it was handled by the Clinic for Special Children in Leacock Township. On August 26, US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested that the deaths were fabricated. “I don’t want to go into details in terms of how we were able to ascertain that information, but I mean, certainly the providers there did not think that it was a case that needed to be referred to the coroner’s office because many of these children end up dying of respiratory infections of different types, and the death was not unexpected," Diamantoni said. Pennsylvania adds 115 new cases Today, the CDC updated the country’s measles case count, which stands at 3,134, including the two Pennsylvania deaths. Eight percent of measles patients have been hospitalized. Of the total, 231 infections are new. That compares with 126 new cases last week. Of all cases, 94% occurred in people who were unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status. All cases but 16 were locally transmitted. In all of 2025, 2,289 measles case were confirmed in the United States. In Pennsylvania, officials today added 115 new cases—about half of all new US infections—from the past week to its state case tally, raising it to 577 cases. None of the state’s cases involve people fully vaccinated against the virus. In total, 98 people (17%) have been hospitalized. Thirty percent of infections occurred in children. The Pennsylvania Department of Health also warned that travelers at the New Stanton Service Plaza on the westbound Pennsylvania Turnpike in Westmoreland County may have been exposed to measles by a person from another state who stopped at the plaza on August 17 and later tested positive for the virus. On the cusp of the Labor Day weekend, which entails travel for many people, healthcare professionals are urging travelers to be vigilant in monitoring for symptoms of the highly contagious disease, such as rash, fever, and red, watery eyes. Ohio is reporting 15 new cases, including five cases in Wayne County, amid its third measles outbreak of the year, raising its tally for the year to 122. news.source_body_en: In Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, a measles-related infant death was confirmed by the coroner, Stephen Diamantoni, MD, on August 18, 2026. This marks the second such death in the county, with the first attributed to a ruptured spleen rather than measles. The CDC has not included these deaths in its 2026 measles fatality count. As of August 26, 2026, the US measles case count reached 3,134, with 115 new cases reported in Pennsylvania. Eight percent of patients were hospitalized, and 94% of cases involved unvaccinated or unknown vaccination status individuals. The Pennsylvania Department of Health warned about potential exposure at the New Stanton Service Plaza on the Pennsylvania Turnpike. The case was initially managed by the Clinic for Special Children before being referred to the coroner’s office. The uncertainty surrounding the infant’s infection timeline remains unresolved, and the broader public health response includes urging vigilance among travelers ahead of the Labor Day weekend.

news.title: New measles cases associated with metro Atlanta day care outbreak confirmed, health officials say
news.excerpt: Health officials have confirmed three new measles cases connected with an outbreak of the virus at a metro Atlanta day care.
news.rss_summary_html: Health officials have confirmed three new measles cases connected with an outbreak of the virus at a metro Atlanta day care.

news.content: Latest U.S. Iran War Lindsay Clancy Trial World Politics Entertainment HealthWatch MoneyWatch Crime Space Sports Brand Studio The Free Press Local News Atlanta Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas Live CBS News 24/7 Baltimore Bay Area Boston Chicago Colorado Detroit Los Angeles Miami Minnesota New York Philadelphia Pittsburgh Sacramento Texas 48 Hours 60 Minutes Shows 48 Hours 60 Minutes CBS Evening News CBS Mornings CBS Morning News CBS Reports CBS Saturday Morning The Daily Report The Dish Face the Nation Sunday Morning The Takeout Things That Matter The Uplift CBS News Investigates CBS News Confirmed Podcasts Newsletters Download Our App CBS News Team Executive Team Brand Studio Paramount+ Join Our Talent Community RSS Feeds Atlanta | News Weather Meet Our Team News Tips Contact Us Download with Damez Download Our App Advertise Memorials Watch CBS News Local News New measles cases associated with metro Atlanta day care outbreak confirmed, health officials say By Dan Raby Dan Raby Senior Digital Producer, CBS News Atlanta Dan Raby, the senior digital producer for CBS News Atlanta, has been covering everything happening around Georgia for more than a decade. Read Full Bio Dan Raby September 4, 2026 / 3:55 PM EDT / CBS Atlanta Add CBS News on Google Georgia health officials have confirmed additional measles cases connected to an outbreak of the virus connected with a metro Atlanta day care. On Friday, the Fulton County Department of Health announced that state officials have confirmed three additional cases associated with the outbreak, which brings the number of cases up to eight. Details about the outbreak remain limited, but Fulton County officials say it "is associated with a daycare setting in the metro Atlanta area" and that the children involved were either unvaccinated or not fully vaccinated. County officials reported the first measles case connected with the outbreak on Aug. 18, then confirmed four additional cases on Aug. 28. Health officials are now working to notify individuals who may have been exposed to the virus with the additional cases. The new update brings the number of confirmed cases of measles in Georgia to 14. This year's number of cases is the second-highest number in the last decade, behind the 18 cases reported in 2019. Data from the Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention shows that more than 2,700 cases of measles have been reported this year, making it the highest number in recent history and putting the country at risk of losing its official measles elimination status. Possible signs of measles exposure and what you should do Measles first infects the respiratory tract, then spreads throughout the body, causing a high fever, runny nose, cough, red, watery eyes, and a rash. The rash generally appears three to five days after the first symptoms, beginning as flat red spots on the face and then spreading downward to the neck, trunk, arms, legs, and feet. When the rash appears, the fever may spike over 104 degrees Fahrenheit, according to the CDC. The virus is highly contagious, spreads through the air, and can stay on surfaces for up to two hours after an infected person has been in a room. If you become sick or believe you have been exposed to measles, contact your healthcare provider immediately but do not go to the doctor's office without first letting them know about your symptoms. You can also call the Georgia Department of Public Health's Acute Disease Epidemiology Section at 404-657-2588 during business hours, Monday through Friday, or 1-866-782-4584 after hours on evenings and weekends. Officials say you should also stay at home and avoid contact with other people, especially anyone younger than 1 year old or those who have weakened immune systems. The Associated Press contributed to this report. news.content: (The Center Square) — A 6-week-old baby girl died from measles last month in Lancaster County, though its unclear if this is the second death identified by the Department of Health during an Aug. 25 press conference that's raised more questions than it answered. First reported by LNP , Lancaster County Coroner Stephen Diamantoni said the infant, born with a rare genetic condition called Amish lethal microcephaly, was in palliative care with an anticipated life expectancy of less than six months. He says he doesn't know if the child was born with measles or contracted it later. The Center Square has not independently confirmed the report. The first identified fatality was a newborn baby, also from the county, who tested positive for measles but died from a ruptured spleen and massive blood loss. Diamantoni said the forensic pathologist did not see any indication that the virus affected the organ. The department said during its Aug. 25 press conference that the deaths are the first related to measles in 35 years. An ongoing outbreak has spread to at least 36 of Pennsylvania's 67 counties, sickening 577 residents and hospitalizing 98. Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro, while announcing the deaths, blasted U.S. Health Secretary Robert Kennedy Jr. for rhetoric and directives that he says have lowered Americans' trust in vaccinations — a sentiment again reiterated at a Thursday press conference in Philadelphia. The MMR vaccine – which stands for Measles, Mumps, and Rubella – isn't administered until infants are at least one year old . An early dose, between 6 and 11 months, is only recommended when active cases exist. A second dose is given before starting elementary school. "I think it's incumbent on the people who had the press conference to provide accurate information," Lancaster County Commissioner Josh Parsons recently told The Center Square . "And that's really the lesson that we learned out of COVID, which is a lot of people are very distrustful of government, very distrustful of medical officials now and health officials, because of what happened during COVID, so you have to be very careful and provide accurate information." An unconfirmed report from The Atlantic identified the family who lost the infant as members of the Amish community. The mother, who requested not to be identified, said she was hospitalized for a severe case of measles just days before she went in labor. Vaccination rates among Amish and Mennonite communities – of which the country's largest concentration lives in Lancaster County – have been historically low , hovering around 25%, according to federal data. "And I think the issue that some have is that they don't like that they choose not to be vaccinated, and you know that's fine," Parsons said. "They cannot like it, but my position is, as American citizens, they have that right to decide that, and we can provide the information that we do. But ultimately, people have the right to decide that." The United Nations General Assembly on Friday endorsed a new world map that represents Africa more accurately in its larger size, a culmination of a recent campaign led by African countries and advocacy groups. Friday’s resolution, which was sponsored by Togo and backed by members of the African Union, was passed with 164 member states voting in favor. The vote encourages governments and institutions around the world to replace the traditional Mercator map, commonly used since the 16th Century, with the Equal Earth projection that advocates and geographers say shows locations more accurately. The Panama Canal on Friday began reducing the number of ships passing through due to a drought caused by the El Nino weather phenomenon.In 2023, El Nino forced the canal authority to reduce the number of daily crossings to 22 vessels. jjr/axm/cb/mlm NFL career rushing leader Emmitt Smith is being sued by a Native American investment company over claims that the former Dallas Cowboys running back and his business partners misappropriated a $2.5 million loan that was supposed to fund a wind farm project in Texas. Kituwah LLC claimed in a lawsuit filed this week in Delaware that 4 13 Solutions used the money to repay an investor from previous dealings with Smith's company. Kituwah's attorneys said Smith and the Pro Football Hall of Famer's longtime business partner, David Mosley, misrepresented their efforts to secure a U.S. Department of Energy loan that would have triggered repayment to Kituwah. Tetris said on Friday that it did not give permission for the White House to use the game's iconic imagery for a controversial online arcade that the Trump administration released on Thursday.The White House released several games Thursday, with a placeholder that teased another one "coming soon." The Homeland Security and Further Additional Continuing Appropriations Act set aside​ $140 million to give controllers a 3.8% pay raise, but they have so far only received the 1% raise given to all government employees. If it wins an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt, it would be the first time a far-right party has held state-level power in Germany since World War Two. With Argentina's President Milei promising "winds of change" over the Falklands, will Donald Trump shift his stance on British rule? A woman who has multiple health issues says she was made to feel she was "telling lies" after being turned down for Personal Independence Payment. The BOP in July entered into an exclusive arrangement with a Florida startup that allows the company to sell federal prisoners nicotine pouches that are not authorized by the FDA. news.content_zh: 据《中心广场》报道,宾夕法尼亚州兰开斯特县一名6周大的女婴因麻疹去世。这起死亡事件发生在上个月,由兰开斯特县验尸官史蒂芬·迪亚蒙托尼在8月25日的新闻发布会上宣布。这名婴儿出生时患有罕见的遗传疾病——阿米什人致命性小头畸形,并接受姑息治疗,预期寿命不足六个月。卫生部门指出,这些死亡是过去35年来首次与麻疹相关。目前,麻疹 暴发已蔓延至宾夕法尼亚州至少36个县,影响了577名居民,其中98人住院治疗。该婴儿的母亲在分娩前几天因麻疹严重病例住院治疗。《中心广场》尚未独立证实该报告,死亡的确切原因以及麻疹病毒是否影响了器官仍不清楚。该报告还指出,阿米什人和门诺会社区的疫苗接种率一直较低,历史平均约为25%。卫生部门批评了美国卫生部长罗伯特·肯尼迪 Jr. 的言论,认为这些言论可能削弱了公众对疫苗接种的信任,这一观点在费城最近的一次新闻发布会上也得到了呼应。

news.excerpt: Many public health experts are alarmed by a decision by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to question two deaths that Pennsylvania officials say are associated with an ongoing measles outbreak.

news.content_title: Experts alarmed by CDC choice to question deaths associated with measles
news.content: Many public health experts are alarmed by a decision by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to question two deaths that Pennsylvania officials say are associated with an ongoing measles outbreak. The deaths would be the first this year linked to a resurgence of measles in the U.S., but instead of listing the deaths on the CDC website as usual, the agency took the highly unusual step of posting a notice that they were reviewing the cases. "That smacks of political interference," said Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, the former director of the CDC's National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases, resigned from the agency last year after clashing with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. "Something's fishy, and this is dangerous." In an email to NPR, a spokeswoman for Kennedy said the information on the CDC's website "reflects the best available information and our commitment to transparency and telling the American people the truth."
